source_excerpt: NEW DELHI: Can being in a long-term relationship or being engaged mean consent to sexual acts? The Himachal Pradesh high court has ruled that a relationship does not give one partner the right to force sexual acts on the other, denying anticipatory bail to a man accused of sexually assaulting and physically abusing his fiancÃ©e. The court also flagged gaps in the state's medico-legal report format used in sexual offence cases.In its October 12, 2026, order, the high court noted that the medical report recorded injuries and burn marks on the woman. It also raised concerns over the absence of a column for recording the nature and probable duration of injuries in the new format.Why did the man seek anticipatory bail?As per the court order, the woman told police that she had been living with her fiancÃ© in Manali since May 2026. She alleged that he had injured her neck earlier and that they had returned to Manali in August after spending time away.The woman alleged that on August 23, the man abused and assaulted her, sexually assaulted her against her will, burned her private parts with a lighter and choked her. An FIR was registered on August 25 under Sections 64(1), 115(2) and 351(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which deal with rape, voluntarily causing hurt and criminal intimidation, respectively.The man sought anticipatory bail, claiming he had been falsely implicated. His counsel argued that the complaint was filed two days after the alleged incident and that the medical report did not support the allegations of burns.The woman's counsel opposed the plea, arguing that the medical report recorded injuries and burn marks. The woman also alleged that the man had tried to pressure and intimidate her and other witnesses after seeking bail.Why did the high court deny anticipatory bail?Justice Chirag Bhanu Singh noted that the couple had been in a long relationship and were engaged. However, it said the medical report recorded injuries on the woman's thighs, around her breast and on her forearms, along with burn marks on her thighs.The court said the delay in reporting the incident was not fatal to the prosecution's case at this stage, given the nature of the relationship. It also considered the allegations that the man had tried to pressure the woman and witnesses.âEven if in a relationship, it did not give him a license to ravish the prosecutrix sexually and that too, in such a barbaric way. âNoâ had to mean a âNoâ,â the court observed.The high court dismissed the anticipatory bail plea, while observing that the man might have a case for regular bail. It clarified that its observations were limited to deciding the bail application and were not a final finding on the merits of the case.What problem did the court flag in medical reports?The high court also raised concerns about the new format of medico-legal reports (MLCs) being used in sexual offence cases across Himachal Pradesh. It found that the report in this case did not contain a specific column for the doctor's opinion on the nature of the injuries or their probable duration.The probable duration of injuries can help investigators and courts assess whether medical findings are consistent with the timeline described in a complaint. The court noted that the doctor had not given an opinion on the duration of the injuries in this case.âNon-recording of the probable duration of injuries as an Expert has an important bearing on the case,â the court said.The bench advised the state to correct the format or continue using the earlier version, which included these details. It also directed the prosecution to seek the doctor's opinion on the probable duration of the injuries in this case.The court highlighted the importance of recording these medical details to help assess the timing and nature of injuries. It clarified that its observations on the report format were intended to flag the need for corrective measures and did not decide the final outcome of the criminal case.
